title: Design a Vending Machine
statement_md:
*Gang of Four pattern: **State** (behavioral). The machine's rules live in its
states, not in the methods.*

Design a coin-operated `VendingMachine`. The machine is always in exactly one of
three states, and **every method behaves differently depending on which one**:

- `"IDLE"` — no credit inserted.
- `"HAS_CREDIT"` — credit has been inserted but no item is waiting.
- `"DISPENSING"` — an item has been paid for and is waiting to be taken.

Implement the `VendingMachine` class:

- `VendingMachine(items)` stocks the machine. Each entry of `items` is
  `[name, price, quantity]`, with prices and coins in cents. Names are distinct.
  The machine starts in `"IDLE"` with zero credit.
- `insertCoin(coin)` accepts a coin worth `5`, `10`, `25`, or `100` cents, adding
  it to the credit and returning `"OK"`. Returns `"REJECTED"` — leaving the credit
  unchanged — if `coin` is any other value, or if the machine is `"DISPENSING"`
  (it can't take money until the paid item is taken).
- `select(name)` attempts to buy one unit of `name`. It returns the **first** of
  these that applies, checked in this order:
  - `"BUSY"` if the machine is `"DISPENSING"`.
  - `"UNKNOWN_ITEM"` if `name` was never stocked.
  - `"SOLD_OUT"` if its remaining quantity is `0`.
  - `"NO_CREDIT"` if the machine is `"IDLE"`.
  - `"INSUFFICIENT_CREDIT"` if the credit is less than the price.
  - Otherwise `"OK"`: the price is deducted from the credit, the quantity drops
    by one, and the machine moves to `"DISPENSING"`.
- `dispense()` hands over the item bought by the last successful `select`,
  returning its name. Change is **not** returned automatically — the machine
  moves to `"HAS_CREDIT"` if any credit remains, otherwise `"IDLE"`. Returns
  `"NOTHING_SELECTED"` if the machine isn't `"DISPENSING"`.
- `refund()` returns all remaining credit as an integer (`0` if there is none)
  and moves the machine to `"IDLE"`. Returns `-1` and changes nothing if the
  machine is `"DISPENSING"` — the paid item must be taken first.
- `getState()` returns the current state name.

Every operation should run in `O(1)` time.
constraints: $1 \le \texttt{name.length} \le 10$, lowercase letters and digits; names are distinct
At most $10^4$ calls will be made to `insertCoin`, `select`, `dispense`, `refund`, and `getState`.

solutions.title: Conditional Dispatch on a State Flag
solutions.intuition_md:
The machine is a finite state machine, so the most direct translation is to
store the state as a plain string and branch on it inside every method. This
works and is `O(1)`, and it's worth writing once to see exactly what the state
rules are before hiding them behind anything.

The cost isn't speed, it's structure: the transition table ends up smeared
across five methods, and nothing keeps them consistent. Adding a fourth state
(a `"MAINTENANCE"` mode, say) means finding and correctly extending every
`if`/`elif` chain — and the compiler won't tell you which one you missed.
solutions.algorithm_md:
Keep `credit`, a `pending` item name, `stock`/`price` dicts, and a `state`
string. Each method opens by testing `state` and returns the appropriate refusal
before touching anything.

- `insertCoin`: refuse while `"DISPENSING"` or on a bad denomination; otherwise
  add the coin and set `state = "HAS_CREDIT"`.
- `select`: run the six checks in the order the statement specifies. The
  `"IDLE"` test is what distinguishes `"NO_CREDIT"` from `"INSUFFICIENT_CREDIT"`
  — both mean "not enough money", but only one of them is a state.
- `dispense`: only legal while `"DISPENSING"`; the next state depends on whether
  change is left over, which is why it's computed rather than hard-coded.
- `refund`: legal in either non-dispensing state, so it needs no branch beyond
  rejecting `"DISPENSING"`.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Every method is a fixed number of dict lookups and comparisons; nothing iterates over the inventory or the call history.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Two dicts sized by the number of distinct items, plus a constant amount of machine state.

solutions.title: State Pattern (One Class Per State)
solutions.intuition_md:
The Gang of Four's State pattern turns the branch inside-out: instead of every
method asking "which state am I in?", each *state* becomes an object that knows
how to handle every action. The machine holds a reference to its current state
object and delegates each call to it; a transition is one assignment,
`m.state = HAS_CREDIT`.

The payoff is that the transition table becomes readable as a table — one class
per state, one method per action, so the rules for `"DISPENSING"` all sit in one
place instead of being scattered across five `elif` arms. A base `State` class
whose methods all refuse gives every state a safe default, so a concrete state
only overrides the actions it actually permits, and an unhandled action can
never silently fall through to the wrong behaviour.

The trade-off is real, not free: three extra classes and a level of indirection
buy nothing for a two-state machine. The pattern earns its keep once the number
of state-dependent actions times the number of states is large enough that
keeping the `elif` chains in sync becomes the actual bug source.
solutions.algorithm_md:
Define a `State` base class with one method per action (`insertCoin`, `select`,
`dispense`, `refund`), each taking the machine as an argument since the states
are stateless and shared. The base implementations are the refusals — `select`
returns `"BUSY"`, `dispense` returns `"NOTHING_SELECTED"` — so a subclass only
writes the actions its state allows.

- `Idle` overrides `insertCoin` (accept, move to `HasCredit`) and `select`
  (report `"UNKNOWN_ITEM"`/`"SOLD_OUT"` first, then `"NO_CREDIT"`).
- `HasCredit` overrides `insertCoin` (accept, stay put) and `select` (the full
  purchase path, moving to `Dispensing`).
- `Dispensing` overrides `dispense` (hand over `pending`, then move to
  `HasCredit` or `Idle` depending on leftover change) and `refund` (return `-1`),
  and inherits the base refusals for `insertCoin` and `select`.

Instantiate each state once as a module-level singleton — they carry no
per-machine data, so there's no reason to allocate a new one per transition.
`VendingMachine`'s own methods then shrink to one-line delegations, and
`getState` just reports `self.state.name`.
solutions.time_complexity_reason: Identical work to the flag version plus one attribute lookup for the delegation — the pattern changes where the branch lives, not how much work it does.
solutions.space_complexity_reason: Same two inventory dicts. The three state objects are module-level singletons shared by every machine, so they add a constant, not a per-instance cost.
